19 The diagram shows a block on a slope.
8.0 m
h
1.8 N
A constant force of 1.8 N in a direction parallel to the slope is exerted on the block. This causes
the block to move along the slope at a constant speed.
The block moves a distance of 8.0 m along the slope and gains height h. The work done against
the frictional force acting on the block is 4.8 J.
The weight of the block is 4.0 N.
What is the value of h?
A
1.2 m
B
2.4 m
C
3.6 m
D
4.8 m

hints: Notice the $1.8\text{ N}$ force is parallel to the $8.0\text{ m}$ displacement up the slope, so calculate the total work it puts in.
Because speed is constant, that input work does not become kinetic energy but is split into work against friction ($4.8\text{ J}$) and gain in gravitational potential energy.
Set the remaining energy equal to $Wh$ with weight $4.0\text{ N}$ and solve for the vertical height $h$.
walkthrough: Work done by the constant parallel force is $W_{in} = Fd$. With $F = 1.8\text{ N}$ and $d = 8.0\text{ m}$, $W_{in} = 1.8 \times 8.0 = 14.4\text{ J}$.
The block moves at constant speed, so kinetic energy does not change. The $14.4\text{ J}$ input must appear as useful gravitational potential energy plus work against friction.
Work against friction is given as $4.8\text{ J}$, so gain in gravitational potential energy is $E_p = 14.4 - 4.8 = 9.6\text{ J}$.
Gravitational potential gain is $E_p = Wh$ where weight $W = 4.0\text{ N}$. So $4.0 \times h = 9.6$.
Hence $h = 9.6 / 4.0 = 2.4\text{ m}$. This is option B.

A.explanation: This gives $4.8\text{ J}$ of gravitational potential energy, which equals only the work against friction and ignores the extra $9.6\text{ J}$ from the $1.8\text{ N}$ push.

B.explanation: Input work $14.4\text{ J}$ minus $4.8\text{ J}$ against friction leaves $9.6\text{ J}$ of $Wh$, giving $h = 2.4\text{ m}$.

C.explanation: This gives $14.4\text{ J}$ of gravitational potential energy, which is the total input work with no subtraction for the $4.8\text{ J}$ lost to friction.

D.explanation: This gives $19.2\text{ J}$ of gravitational potential energy, which incorrectly adds the $4.8\text{ J}$ of frictional work to the $14.4\text{ J}$ input.
